findings.quantum_threat: Shor's algorithm factors the modulus n in polynomial time on a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). Every RSA key size — 2048 or 4096 — falls to the same attack.
findings.description: RSA-2048 is used for session-token signing. A quantum adversary can forge signatures and impersonate the token issuer, fully compromising authentication.
findings.snippet:
from Crypto.PublicKey import RSA
key = RSA.generate(2048)
signature = pkcs1_5.sign(token, key)

recommendation.note: Drop-in signature replacement. Signature size grows 2420 B vs 256 B — verify token length limits.

findings.quantum_threat: Shor's algorithm breaks RSA at any key size. 1024-bit is additionally within reach of well-funded classical adversaries today.
findings.description: Short RSA key used for license verification. Broken pre-quantum by key size alone; trivially broken post-quantum.

recommendation.note: Replace immediately; interim classical fix is RSA-3072, but that is also quantum-broken.

findings.quantum_threat: Shor's algorithm solves the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem, recovering the private key from the public key.
findings.description: ECDSA signs payment authorisation requests. Quantum key recovery lets an attacker authorise arbitrary transactions.
findings.snippet:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import ecdsa
private_key = ec.generate_private_key(ec.SECP256R1())
sig = private_key.sign(payload, ec.ECDSA(hashes.SHA256()))

recommendation.note: SPHINCS+ offers conservative security from hash functions alone; ML-DSA if signature size matters more.

findings.quantum_threat: Shor's algorithm breaks the elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman problem, exposing every session key negotiated by it.
findings.description: Key agreement for the message channel. Recorded traffic can be decrypted retroactively once a CRQC exists ('harvest now, decrypt later').

recommendation.note: Faster handshake than ECDH; public key 1184 B. Pair with a hybrid X25519+ML-KEM during transition.

findings.quantum_threat: Shor's algorithm solves the finite-field discrete logarithm. 1024-bit groups are also within classical nation-state reach.
findings.description: Legacy DH parameter negotiation for admin console sessions.

recommendation.note: Remove finite-field DH entirely rather than raising group size — larger groups stay quantum-broken.

findings.quantum_threat: Already broken classically — practical collision attacks since 2004. No quantum computer needed.
findings.description: MD5 checksum for file integrity. Collisions allow tampered files to pass verification.

recommendation.note: One-line change; SHA-2 is Grover-resistant at 384+ bits.

findings.quantum_threat: Collision attack demonstrated by Google/CWI in 2017 (SHAttered). Deprecated by NIST since 2011.
findings.description: SHA-1 used for legacy commit verification fallback.

recommendation.note: Drop the legacy fallback branch entirely.

findings.quantum_threat: 64-bit block size enables Sweet32 birthday attacks on long sessions. Formally deprecated by NIST in 2023.
findings.description: Legacy configuration store decryption. Small block size leaks information across large payloads.

recommendation.note: Authenticated encryption also removes the separate MAC pass. Same JCA call shape.

findings.quantum_threat: ECB mode leaks structure — identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks (the 'ECB penguin'). Grover further halves the 128-bit security margin.
findings.description: Card PAN data encrypted in ECB mode. Patterns in card numbers remain visible in ciphertext.
findings.snippet:
from Crypto.Cipher import AES
cipher = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_ECB)

recommendation.note: GCM provides confidentiality + integrity together; 256-bit key restores the Grover margin.

findings.quantum_threat: Not an algorithm weakness — the key itself is in source control. Anyone with repo access can decrypt production data today.
findings.description: AES key embedded as a string literal in source. Detectable by every secret-scanner; already exposed to every developer who ever cloned the repo.

recommendation.note: Rotate the key, store in AWS KMS / HashiCorp Vault, and load at runtime. Not a PQC issue — fix today.

findings.quantum_threat: The private key is committed in source. Combined with F-001, an attacker can forge tokens right now — no quantum computer required.
findings.description: RSA private key PEM block in source code used as a signing fallback.

recommendation.note: Rotate the keypair immediately, purge from git history, and provision via KMS.

findings.quantum_threat: TLS 1.1 was formally deprecated in RFC 8996 (2021). Weak ciphersuites and no modern handshake protection.
findings.description: HTTPS client pinned to TLS 1.1 for an internal metrics endpoint.

recommendation.note: TLS 1.3 disables the legacy ciphersuites; PQC hybrids are already shipping in Chrome/OpenSSL.

findings.quantum_threat: CBC without proper MAC is malleable; 192-bit key leaves only a 96-bit Grover margin (still strong).
findings.description: Internal cache encryption. Not urgent, but CBC malleability means tampering is undetected without a separate MAC.

recommendation.note: Swap mode to GCM in the next release cycle.

findings.quantum_threat: Certificate uses RSA-2048 SubjectPublicKeyInfo — inherits RSA's quantum exposure. Also self-signed and expiring 2027-03.
findings.description: Self-signed service certificate with an RSA public key, expiring March 2027.

recommendation.note: On renewal, use a composite classical+PQC SPKI; cert chains are the slowest thing on the internet to rotate.

findings.quantum_threat: Grover's algorithm halves key search, leaving an effective 128-bit margin — beyond any feasible attack, classical or quantum.
findings.description: Primary data-at-rest encryption. Correctly used authenticated encryption with a 256-bit key.
findings.snippet:
cipher = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_GCM, nonce=nonce)
ciphertext, tag = cipher.encrypt_and_digest(data)

recommendation.note: Quantum-safe as deployed. Keep the key in a KMS (see F-010 for the contrast).

findings.quantum_threat: Grover reduces preimage resistance to 128 bits — still infeasible.
256-bit key retains a 128-bit Grover margin; AEAD construction is quantum-safe.
findings.description: Real-time channel encryption. Modern AEAD cipher.

findings.quantum_threat: HMAC's security relies on the PRF property of SHA-256, which Grover does not meaningfully weaken at 256-bit output.
